I found this in Helix log:

2026-10-09T16:38:29.278 helix_lsp::transport [ERROR] roc-experimental <- ServerError(-32803): Semantic features require initializationOptions.trustedWorkspace: true; restart the server after granting trust.
This is very bad UX.
I don't see anything in the Helix interface, I have to dig through logs.
I don't even know whether it's some Roc setting to tweak, or a Helix setting.
Is there some documentation about it?
It's in a project that I developed from scratch, not something I downloaded.
It's probably to do with this PR. I don't use Helix, but I suspect the command :workspace-trust might be what you need
Yes I picked this up in a review of CVE's as something we should fix to prevent untrusted codebases doing nefarious things through the LSP
Thanks, @Jonathan. That's it. I'm using the stable release of Helix, which does not have this feature yet, so it was not showing the trust modal nor the warning sign.
Is it possible to detect the editor name from the LSP?

Since many users are using the latest stable Helix, which does not have the "workspace trust" feature, maybe a window/showMessage could help them understand what's happening, and how they can resolve it.

I'm using the stable release of Helix, which does not have this feature yet, so it was not showing the trust modal nor the warning sign.

there might be some way in LSP to do feature detection?
There is, but I think this workspace trust thing is not detectable via that.

The unfortunate thing is that Helix has been abandoned by its original author, so no new releases can be expected, and I don't know how much time it takes for Linux distros to switch to a maintained fork.
ok so let's say we communicate it via a message...what would Helix users be able to do?

I just hardcoded the trust value into the Roc LSP initial settings:

[language-server.roc-experimental]
command = "roc"
args = ["experimental-lsp"]
config = { "trustedWorkspace" = true }
Explaining this is not doable via a simple message. I recommend directing them towards some kind of documentation page.
Helix does not support workspace trusting yet. Compile Helix from the master branch, or see https://roc-lang.org/helix for workaround on stable release.

But this is too long, maybe just print the link:

To enable semantic analysis, see https://roc-lang.org/helix for instructions.
that seems reasonable, although I'd like to have the link go somewhere else...I don't really want to have a roc-lang.org/helix page indefinitely :sweat_smile:
Not needed indefinitely, just until a new Helix release or most of the distros switching to the maintained unofficial fork.
But I understand the concern.
Could use any URL shortener instead, pointed to a GitHub Pages link.
But the official domain signals trust.
Is there any “editor support” page at all in the documentation?
New tools/languages usually include one.
not currently, but I guess we could add a section

See these for example:
https://biomejs.dev/configuration/editors/
https://zine-ssg.io/docs/editors/
Would you better agree to a https://roc-lang.org/editors/helix link?
I guess N is pretty small for total number of editors we'd have on there, so yeah let's go for it :thumbs_up:
I'll put together a guide for Helix.
@notramo we could add something to https://github.com/lukewilliamboswell/roc-awesome
The lack of development activity around Helix is quite annoying, and many users feel this way. Unfortunately, it's putting the burden on projects like Roc and other languages.
Setting up Roc on a clean Helix config is a task on its own.
probably worth adding to the new page then!
if anyone wants to make a PR to the website to just get some information up there, we can figure out the styling etc in follow-ups

{"code":-32803,"message":"Semantic features require initializationOptions.trustedWorkspace: true; restart the server after granting trust.","data":null}}

I also got it working again in nvim with this config (using lazy):

  {
    "neovim/nvim-lspconfig",
    opts = {
      servers = {
        roc = {
          cmd = { "roc", "experimental-lsp" },
          filetypes = { "roc" },
          init_options = {
            trustedWorkspace = true,
          },
          mason = false,
        },
      },
    },
  }

in theory those operations should be harmless aside from wasting disk space and/or heating up your CPU
In practice, there could be exploits.
yeah originating from compiler bugs etc
But there's not really a difference between running the code in the LSP and running it in roc check or roc run.

and regardless it seems like better practice to only download potentially large things from untrusted sources (and run arbitrarily cpu-intensive work) only with permission, but yeah if it's not implemented by clients in practice then not worth it for now :+1:
I'll change it - can someone open an issue to track this and link to this conversation?

Practically nobody does this specific workflow where this workspace trust feature would be an improvement:

  • Clone an untrusted repo. Known to be untrusted, otherwise the user simply grants trust in the editor modal.
  • Edit the code, with LSP enabled (but no eval).
  • Do not run roc check or roc run or roc build on the code, ever!
Issue: https://github.com/roc-lang/roc/issues/12784
@notramo this would happen from just viewing the code even if you're not editing it, that's the concern
so like you clone a repo just to look at the code and lsp starts doing this stuff
Users rarely clone a potentially dangerous repo locally just to look at potentially dangerous code in the editor.
In most cases they also run code that they downloaded.
If I would clone an untrusted Roc repo, I would probably never run Helix, and instead use a pager to look at the code. Or not even clone it, but inspect it in the web UI of the Git hosting platform.
The problem is that this LSP config gives users a false sense of security.
It's the wrong boundary to use for security.
If a repo is potentially dangerous, it's a whole other problem, users should probably not even clone it!
I think the origin of the motivating issue came from a review of CVE's from other projects ... so it wasn't a hypothetical issue but something from another project.

Yes, but if an actual CVE were found, I would recommend:

  • Completely uninstall the affected Roc compiler version, so it can't be started accidentally.
  • Do not clone a potentially dangerous repo.
It was CVE-2026-34060 I think

CVE review behind Roc issue #11902

Issue #11902 (https://github.com/roc-lang/roc/issues/11902) came from reviewing CVE-2026-34060, a Ruby LSP code-injection vulnerability (https://github.com/Shopify/ruby-lsp/security/advisories/GHSA-c4r5-fxqw-vh93). Ruby LSP inserted a workspace-controlled setting into a generated Gemfile, allowing a malicious project to execute code when opened in an editor.

The review identified a related trust concern in Roc: opening a file triggered dependency downloads and native compile-time evaluation without an explicit workspace-trust opt-in.

Roc did not share Ruby LSP’s injection defect. The review classified the concern as “weakness possible”, since escaping Roc’s effect-free compile-time evaluation would require an additional compiler or runtime bug.
^^ a quick summary made by Codex
Yes, but the practicality of it is nearly zero.
Not to mention the UX aspect of warning fatigue. Users get used to the dialog and their muscle memory gets trained to grant the trust.

It's a terrible security boundary, and nobody should rely on it.

  • If the code is dangerous, much more serious security measures must be taken (e.g. not cloning; using pager instead of editor; uninstall known vulnerable Roc versions).
  • If it's trusted, this brings nothing, but UX inconvenience. Users are going to roc check or roc run trusted packages, or grant the trust anyways, to get "goto definition" or type info.

We can document that CTFE must be effect-free to control for any malicious code limited to those harmless things. Then if we find a compiler bug in future that can be exploited we have a concrete vulnerability to report and address.
CTFE must be effect-free for many other reasons too.
Nobody wants code that behaves differently based on which machine it was compiled on.
I agree that running arbitrary code from an untrusted source is just asking for trouble and there are few ways to control the risks from that -- even with Roc's platform abstraction and purity.
Also, don't forget that if there's a hidden and undiscovered exploit in code that is trusted by the users, this measure is useless, because users are going to trust the repo via the dialog.
It's not reasonable to expect there will never be any exploitable vulnerabilities in the compiler or cli. It's possible there may be something there that hasn't been discovered yet.
I never said that we should not expect it to exist.
I wrote that before your message, was just finishing a thought from above not responding to you there.
I said that it's practically zero probability to this feature being the boundary that stops an exploit in a practical workflow.
